column8: Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Vimmy Ridge, fought from the 9th to the 12th of April 1917, between the Canadian Corps and the German Sixth Army.

Battle of Vimmy Ridge. On Easter Monday, the 9th of April 1917, the four divisions of the Canadian Corps attacked together for the first time, against a ridge in northern France that the Germans had held since 1914. This introduction separates what the records show from what we have reconstructed for the map. Watch the colour of each tag.

The ridge. Vimmy Ridge rises gently from the west and falls steeply on its east side to the Douai plain. Its highest point, Hill 145, looks out over the coalfields of Lens and the German rear. The French lost tens of thousands of men attacking it in 1915. The British took over in 1916 and fought a war underground, of mines and craters. In October 1916 the Canadians arrived. Whoever held the crest could see everything that moved for miles. That is why it mattered.

The plan. Vimmy was the northern part of a larger British offensive at Arras. The Canadians' task was to take the ridge and guard the left flank of the Third Army's attack to the south. Their commander, Lieutenant-General Sir Julian Byng, planned the attack in four stages, each marked on the map by a coloured line: Black, Red, Blue and Brown. The whole ridge was to be taken in about six hours. Every man rehearsed his part on a full-size copy of the battlefield, laid out with tape and flags behind the lines. By the day of the attack, all ranks knew just where they had to go.

The defenders. Three German divisions held the ridge: Bavarians at Thélus, Prussians of the 79th Reserve Division at Vimmy, and the 16th Bavarian Division opposite Souchez. Their front line was a maze of trenches and deep dug-outs. Behind it ran a second line along the crest, and a third on the plain. But their reserve divisions waited fifteen miles back, too far to help in the first hours.

The Germans fell back to a new line on the plain. The ridge stayed in Allied hands for the rest of the war. Vimmy was a local victory inside a larger battle at Arras that did not break through. Four months later the Canadians were still fighting near Lens. For the first time, all four Canadian divisions had fought together. Arthur Currie, who led the 1st Division, soon commanded the whole Corps. In Canada, Vimmy became a symbol of the nation's coming of age. Historians debate how much of that was the battle, and how much the meaning given to it later. On Hill 145 today stands the Canadian National Vimmy Memorial, with the names of more than eleven thousand Canadians killed in France who have no known grave. ---
